rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 (Methodology) <U+2013> the study reports its own documentary review of J<U+00FA>car basin plans, allegations and media, and a participatory action research programme of six meetings/workshops (Table 1), with own results in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 (Figs. 3-6) and ARJ diversion data in Fig. 2.
rows.notes: The study does not measure any reduction in irrigation water consumption attributable to drip. Its own results concern how basin plans (1998, 2014, 2015, 2022 PHJ) estimated and reallocated hypothetical savings (e.g. 120 hm3 earmarked for new irrigable areas in Castilla-La Mancha in 1998; later the 3037 m3/ha/yr 'saving' deducted from ARJ rights for the Albufera), stakeholder perceptions, and a descriptive series of water diverted by the ARJ (Fig. 2) that merely stabilises at ~200 hm3 after modernisation; the 40% lower diversion in the 2006-08 drought is attributed to the main pressurised pipeline, not plot-level drip. The authors explicitly frame these savings as theoretical 'paper water', note that reductions in diversion are offset by lost return flows (rebound effect), state that the guarantee-of-supply benefit of localised irrigation could not be validated, and call for monitoring because actual data are lacking. Quantified savings are cited from Ruiz-Rodr<U+00ED>guez (2017) and Pool et al. (2021). The study is therefore not own evidence that drip effectively reduced consumption; the 'conditions for expanding irrigated farmland' part reflects the planning practice the paper criticises rather than a demonstrated effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 and Sections 3.1-3.2 <U+2013> own documentary review and participatory action research (Table 1; Figs. 3-6; Fig. 2 ARJ diversion data).
rows.notes: The study does not measure groundwater recharge, infiltration or groundwater levels. In the participatory diagnosis (Section 3.2.1, Fig. 3) stakeholders classified the decrease in surface return flows and the reduction in aquifer recharge as very negative effects of drip adoption, and the 2015 basin plan is documented as admitting that modernisation savings affect adjacent aquifers and water bodies. However, the quantification of reduced return flows and recharge is attributed to cited work (Ruiz-Rodr<U+00ED>guez 2017; Pool et al. 2021, 2022), and the authors state that the effect on wetland springs 'has not yet been quantified'. The study's own contribution on this effect is a stakeholder-agreed perception and policy documentation, not a measured or modelled result, so it is not own evidence of harm to groundwater recharge. The claim's arid-area groundwater-level context is also not addressed (semi-arid Mediterranean coastal wetland).

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 and Sections 3.1-3.2 <U+2013> own documentary review and participatory action research (Table 1; Figs. 3-6).
rows.notes: The study contains no data on plant height, harvest weight or yield for any crop. It is a water-planning and governance study of drip adoption in the Acequia Real del J<U+00FA>car and its effects on the Albufera wetland. The only production-related statement is a cited estimate (Ruiz-Rodr<U+00ED>guez et al., 2017) that drip raises farm income by about 800 EUR/ha, reported as a stakeholder argument, not as the study's own result. The claim is misattributed to this source.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a mixed documentary-review and participatory-action-research paper on water accounting, allocation and co-design of corrective measures around drip irrigation adoption in the ARJ (Valencia, Spain); it reports no agronomic or hydrological measurements of its own, and its core thesis questions the water-saving paradigm of drip irrigation (rebound effect, 'paper water').
